item.title: Malimali denied full access to witnesses, given no notice of allegations – Judge
item.description: Former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali was given no notice of the allegations she faced despite natural justice requiring the Commission of Inquiry to clearly inform her of the aspects of her conduct being investigated, the High Court has found. Justice Dane Tuiqereqere made the finding in his judgment quashing the COI findings and declaring the report null and void.
item.content:encoded:
Former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali was given no notice of the allegations she faced despite natural justice requiring the Commission of Inquiry to clearly inform her of the aspects of her conduct being investigated, the High Court has found.

Justice Dane Tuiqereqere made the finding in his judgment quashing the COI findings and declaring the report null and void.

The judge said Malimali was a central person in the inquiry and faced obvious risks to her reputation and career, making it critical that she was afforded a significant level of transparency and participation.

Justice Tuiqereqere said natural justice required Malimali to receive details of the aspects of her conduct that the COI was specifically investigating.

She was also entitled to disclosure of all relevant information collected by the Commission, with that material provided well before the hearings began so she had adequate time to consider it.

The judge said Malimali should also have been given full access to hear and cross-examine all witnesses, rather than only those the Commission allowed her to question.

“Ms Malimali received none of the above,” Justice Tuiqereqere said.

“She was provided no notice of the allegations she faced.”

Instead, the court found Malimali and her counsel were left to work out what areas the COI intended to investigate from a large volume of material supplied only days before the hearings began.

“It was left to her and her counsel to glean from the voluminous material supplied days before the hearings commenced, as to the areas the COI intended to investigate,” the judgment states.

Justice Tuiqereqere also found Malimali did not receive full disclosure of witness evidence and was denied full access to hear or cross-examine all witnesses.

The judgment says Malimali was excluded from hearing the evidence of at least 11 witnesses.

Justice Tuiqereqere said there was also no adequate explanation for why Malimali had restricted access to hearing and cross-examining certain witnesses or why some evidence was heard in closed sessions.

These issues formed part of the court’s consideration of whether the COI had complied with the requirements of procedural fairness and natural justice before making adverse findings against Malimali.

item.title: Graham Leung, Barbara Malimali lost jobs without seeing COI report – Judge
item.description: Former Attorney-General Graham Leung and former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali lost their positions on the basis of adverse findings in the Commission of Inquiry report without having seen the report beforehand, the High Court judgment says. In his ruling quashing the COI findings, Justice Dane Tuiqereqere noted that the inquiry hearings concluded on March 3, 2025, and the applicants heard no
item.content:encoded:
Former Attorney-General Graham Leung and former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali lost their positions on the basis of adverse findings in the Commission of Inquiry report without having seen the report beforehand, the High Court judgment says.

In his ruling quashing the COI findings, Justice Dane Tuiqereqere noted that the inquiry hearings concluded on March 3, 2025, and the applicants heard nothing further from the Commission before its completed report was presented to the President in May.

Justice Tuiqereqere said Leung’s appointment as Attorney-General was terminated on May 30, 2025, on the basis of adverse findings against him.

“He had not seen the COI Report at the time of his termination and was unaware of the adverse findings against him,” the judgment states.

Malimali’s appointment as FICAC Commissioner was revoked on June 2, 2025, also on the basis of adverse findings contained in the report.

Justice Tuiqereqere said Malimali “had not had any opportunity to see the COI Report prior to cessation of her employment”.

The judgment also examined the subsequent public release of the report.

Justice Tuiqereqere said the COI report was released publicly on July 1, 2025, following a decision by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.

“The adverse findings against the applicants were reputationally harmful to the applicants,” the judge said.

“That will have been obvious to the Prime Minister and President.”

Justice Tuiqereqere said none of the applicants was given an opportunity to consider the report or respond to it before its public release.

The court considered whether procedural fairness and natural justice required the applicants to be notified of the adverse findings before the report was completed or released publicly.

In his final declarations, Justice Tuiqereqere found the President and Prime Minister failed to observe the requirements of procedural fairness in relation to the decision to publicly release the report.

The High Court ultimately quashed the adverse findings and recommendations and declared the May 1, 2025 COI report null and void in its entirety.

item.title: Malimali, Clarke, Leung and Vaurasi should have been given chance to respond – Judge
item.description: High Court judge Justice Dane Tuiqereqere says the Commission of Inquiry made “very serious criticisms and findings” against the Barbara Malimali, Graham Leung, Wylie Clarke and Laurel Vaurasi but they were not given notice of draft adverse findings and an opportunity to respond before the report was completed. In his judgment quashing the Commission of Inquiry findings and declaring the report nu
item.content:encoded:
High Court judge Justice Dane Tuiqereqere says the Commission of Inquiry made “very serious criticisms and findings” against the Barbara Malimali, Graham Leung, Wylie Clarke and Laurel Vaurasi but they were not given notice of draft adverse findings and an opportunity to respond before the report was completed.

In his judgment quashing the Commission of Inquiry findings and declaring the report null and void, Justice Tuiqereqere highlighted the seriousness of the conclusions reached against former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali, former Attorney-General Graham Leung, lawyer Laurel Vaurasi and Fiji Law Society President Wylie Clarke.

“The Commissioner made some very serious criticisms and findings against each of the applicants,” Justice Tuiqereqere said.

“The conduct was characterized by the Commissioner as potential criminal offences.”

The judge noted that the criticisms contained in the COI report were not tentative.

“The criticisms were framed as final conclusions and were strongly expressed by the Commissioner,” he said.

Justice Tuiqereqere said none of the four applicants received either a Salmon letter or Maxwellisation notice before the report was finalised.

He said there was a “compelling argument” that Malimali should have received both forms of notice.

“There is a compelling argument that Ms Malimali ought to have received both and that Mr Leung, Ms Vaurasi and Mr Clarke ought to have, at least, received one or other, most likely the latter,” Justice Tuiqereqere said.

The judge explained this would have meant receiving notice of the draft adverse findings and being provided an opportunity to respond before the COI report was completed.

The issue of procedural fairness formed a significant part of the High Court’s findings.

Justice Tuiqereqere ultimately declared that the Commissioner failed to observe procedural fairness before making adverse findings and recommendations against the applicants, thereby denying them natural justice.

The court also ruled that the President and Prime Minister failed to observe procedural fairness in relation to the decision to release the report publicly.

The adverse findings and recommendations were quashed, while the Commission of Inquiry report dated May 1, 2025 was declared null and void in its entirety.

item.title: President, Prime Minister failed to observe procedural fairness: High Court
item.description: The High Court has ruled that the President and Prime Minister failed to observe the requirements of procedural fairness in relation to the decision to release the Commission of Inquiry report to the public. Justice Dane Tuiqereqere made the declaration in his ruling today on judicial review proceedings challenging findings arising from the Commission of Inquiry into the appointment of former FICA
item.content:encoded:
The High Court has ruled that the President and Prime Minister failed to observe the requirements of procedural fairness in relation to the decision to release the Commission of Inquiry report to the public.

Justice Dane Tuiqereqere made the declaration in his ruling today on judicial review proceedings challenging findings arising from the Commission of Inquiry into the appointment of former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali.

In his declarations, Justice Tuiqereqere found that the President, acting on the advice of the Prime Minister, failed to observe procedural fairness when deciding to release the COI report publicly.

The judge said this denied the applicants “a fair and impartial justice”.

Justice Tuiqereqere also ruled that the extension of the Commission of Inquiry after January 31, 2025 was ineffective.

As a result, the Commissioner’s actions after that date, including completion of the report dated May 1, 2025, were declared ultra vires — meaning beyond the Commission’s legal authority.

The court further found that adverse findings and recommendations relating to the September 5, 2024 meeting were outside the scope of the Commission’s terms of reference and therefore unlawful.

Justice Tuiqereqere also found the Commissioner failed to observe procedural fairness before making adverse findings and recommendations against the applicants, thereby denying them natural justice.

The court declared that the Commissioner’s conduct in carrying out the inquiry gave rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias.

The ruling also found certain adverse findings against William Clarke to be irrational, while adverse findings against two other applicants concerning the FICAC office meeting on September 5, 2024 were also declared irrational.

As a result of the declarations, the court quashed the adverse findings and recommendations.

Justice Tuiqereqere further declared the Commission of Inquiry report dated May 1, 2025 “in its entirety, null and void.”

item.title: ‘Nothing to prove’
item.description: DEPUTY Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica says he returns to Cabinet with “nothing to prove”, but with a focus on continuing the economic work he began before spending 10 months outside the executive. Speaking on The Fiji Times online portal The Lens@177, Mr Kamikamica said he remained active during his time outside Cabinet, engaging with investors, micro, small, and medium enterprise operators, and
item.content:encoded:
DEPUTY Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica says he returns to Cabinet with “nothing to prove”, but with a focus on continuing the economic work he began before spending 10 months outside the executive.

Speaking on The Fiji Times online portal The Lens@177, Mr Kamikamica said he remained active during his time outside Cabinet, engaging with investors, micro, small, and medium enterprise operators, and cooperatives.

“In fact, whilst being outside Cabinet, I’ve actually been actively trying to help some outside Cabinet,” he said.

He also chaired the Public Accounts Committee, which he said had done important work in identifying and reporting issues to Government.

Mr Kamikamica said he maintained an open line of communication with Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka throughout his absence, with the PM reaching out to him on various matters.

“He now and again reached out on various things, so that relationship and communication was always open,” he said.

Mr Kamikamica said Government had continued to function during his absence and managed several challenges and crises.

Now back in Cabinet, Mr Kamikamica said his priority was to continue the economic work already underway, rather than prove himself.

“So, not so much anything to prove, but really just continuing where we had left off.”

His focus includes diversifying Fiji’s economy, improving the ease of doing business, and removing constraints affecting businesses.

item.title: Kamikamica feared political career was over
item.description: A criminaL charge and questions over his integrity left Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica wondering whether his political career had come to an end. Mr Kamikamica said there were times when he would sit late at night and wonder what was happening.
item.content:encoded:
A criminaL charge and questions over his integrity left Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica wondering whether his political career had come to an end.

Mr Kamikamica said there were times when he would sit late at night and wonder what was happening.

“When your integrity is questioned and you have a criminal charge against you, you sit late at night sometimes and wonder what’s happening,” he said.

He said entering politics had already been a major sacrifice after coming from the private sector, where he said things were more remunerative.

“Coming to politics was a big sacrifice in itself.”

He said the experience had raised questions about his decision to enter politics.

“Questions around what am I doing here at the time.”

Despite this, Mr Kamikamica said he remained resolute in his belief that Fiji needed rebuilding and that he would continue contributing to that cause.

“And whatever I can do to further that cause whilst I’m in Government, I will continue to do so.”

He credited his upbringing, Christian beliefs, wife, daughter, close family and friends for helping him remain focused and encouraged.

“The amount of prayers across every religion has been quite remarkable.”

Mr Kamikamica said it took a lot for him to shed a tear, although he knew many people had cried on his behalf.

He said the emotional experience was now in the past and that he would keep moving forward.

item.title: Act now, says Ravunawa – Health Ministry sounds alarm over growing HIV epidemic
item.description: IN the next 10 years, one in every classroom could have a child living with HIV if Fiji does nothing to strengthen prevention, Assistant Minister for Health Penioni Ravunawa has warned. Mr Ravunawa’s comments come as Fiji’s HIV epidemic continues to attract international attention, with recent reports describing the country as having one of the fastest-growing HIV epidemics globally.
item.content:encoded:
IN the next 10 years, one in every classroom could have a child living with HIV if Fiji does nothing to strengthen prevention, Assistant Minister for Health Penioni Ravunawa has warned.

Mr Ravunawa’s comments come as Fiji’s HIV epidemic continues to attract international attention, with recent reports describing the country as having one of the fastest-growing HIV epidemics globally.

The growing crisis has also been linked to injecting methamphetamine, with concerns raised about access to safe injecting equipment, HIV prevention and stigma-free healthcare.

The scale of the crisis is reflected in the latest Ministry of Health figures, with Fiji recording 2016 new HIV diagnoses in 2025. The ministry also recorded 117 HIV-related deaths last year, including 17 children aged under 15. Of those who died, 67 had been diagnosed with HIV in the same year.

Mother-to-child transmission remains a major concern, with 59 babies reported to have been born with HIV in 2025, compared with 31 in 2024.

Mr Ravunawa said the country needed a united response to the growing HIV crisis, with communities, traditional leaders and faith-based organisations playing a critical role.

“If we do nothing about HIV prevention,” he said.

He said the ministry needed the involvement of traditional and faith-based leaders to strengthen HIV awareness and prevention at the community level.

“We need that acceptance from traditional and faith-based leaders, etc,” he said.

He said traditional leaders, chiefs, faith-based organisations, health authorities, and communities all had a role to play in confronting the crisis.

item.title: COI findings quashed, report declared null and Void
item.description: The High Court has quashed the findings of the Commission of Inquiry into the appointment of former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali, declaring the COI report null and void in its entirety. Justice Dane Tuiqereqere handed down the decision following separate judicial review proceedings brought by Malimali, former Attorney-General Graham Leung, Fiji Law Society president Wylie Clarke and lawyer
item.content:encoded:
The High Court has quashed the findings of the Commission of Inquiry into the appointment of former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali, declaring the COI report null and void in its entirety.

Justice Dane Tuiqereqere handed down the decision following separate judicial review proceedings brought by Malimali, former Attorney-General Graham Leung, Fiji Law Society president Wylie Clarke and lawyer Laurel Vaurasi.

The judgment runs to 154 pages and deals with challenges brought by the four applicants against findings made concerning them in the Commission of Inquiry report.

The ruling means the challenged COI findings have been set aside, with the report declared null and void in its entirety.

The Commission of Inquiry had been established to investigate the circumstances surrounding Malimali’s appointment as Commissioner of the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption.

Malimali brought judicial review proceeding HBJ 09/2025, naming the Commission of Inquiry into her appointment, the President of Fiji, the Prime Minister and the Attorney-General as respondents.

A separate proceeding, HBJ 10/2025, was brought by Clarke and Vaurasi, who also named the Commission of Inquiry, the President, the Prime Minister and the Attorney-General as respondents. They were represented by Howards Lawyers.

Leung brought proceeding HBJ 11/2025 against the Commission of Inquiry and the Attorney-General and was represented by Fatiaki Law.

The applicants had separately sought judicial review of findings concerning them arising from the inquiry into Malimali’s appointment.

The High Court’s decision represents a major development in the controversy surrounding the COI report and the consequences that followed its findings.

The full implications of the ruling, including Justice Tuiqereqere’s reasoning for quashing the findings and declaring the report null and void, are contained in the 154-page judgment.
